title: Escaping the Diversity Trap via Anchor-Centric Adaptation
one_liner: When teaching a robot a task with limited real-world examples, focus first on repeating demonstrations at a few core positions, then selectively add examples at tricky boundary spots, instead of spreading examples across diverse positions.
lead: Real robots need real-world practice to be reliable. When you have a limited budget of robot demonstrations, the naive instinct is to make them as diverse as possible: try the task from many different angles and starting points. But this paper reveals a trap: that diversity itself becomes the enemy, because when each starting position has only one or two examples, the robot's training is swamped by random noise rather than learning the true task. The paper proposes a two-stage strategy: first, repeat demonstrations at a handful of core positions to build a stable base, then add examples only at the hardest boundaries.

paras: A robot model trained on general internet data (a vision-language-action model) knows a lot but needs real-world practice on your specific hardware. You have a small budget: maybe 100 real-robot demonstrations. The naive strategy is to spread them out: try the task from 100 different starting positions, grippers, and angles. This maximizes coverage, the range of conditions the robot has seen.

But here is the trap: each starting position has only one example. When the robot is training, it sees the one demonstration and tries to match it. Random noise in the camera, the gripper, and the robot's motors is always present. With only one example per position, the robot cannot tell signal from noise. It memorizes random wobbles as if they were the real task. The noise is so large relative to the signal that learning becomes unstable, and the robot fails more often than it would if it had fewer but more repeated examples.

callout.html: Spreading a small budget across many diverse conditions introduces too much noise per condition, so the robot memorizes random details instead of learning the true task.

panels.title: 1. Limited budget
panels.caption: Robot has 100 real-world examples, one choice: spread wide or go deep.

panels.title: 2. Spread wide: one demo per position
panels.caption: Each of 100 positions has one example; noise drowns out the signal.

panels.title: 3. Go deep: repeat at anchors
panels.caption: 10 core positions get 10 demos each; signal emerges from repetition.

panels.title: 4. Mine boundaries
panels.caption: Use the stable base to spot where the robot still struggles most.

panels.title: 5. Selective expansion
panels.caption: Add examples only at high-error boundaries; coverage grows on signal.

steps.text: Choose a small set of core starting positions (e.g., 10 anchors). Collect 10 demos at each.
Use flow matching (gradual denoising) to train the robot on the anchor dataset. The repetition drowns out noise.
Sample probe trajectories across the workspace by joystick control; do not use the base robot yet, just collect sensor observations.

For each probe, feed the sensor image to the stable base robot and see what action it outputs. Compare to the human-demonstrated action on that same image. Large disagreement means the base robot is uncertain and risky there.
Collect new real-robot demos at high-disagreement boundaries using a small learnable adjustment (low-rank adapter). Core stays frozen.

paras: The paper changes the allocation strategy: instead of spreading N total demonstrations uniformly across N positions (one per position), it allocates them as repeated clusters at a small set of anchor positions, then adds selective boundary examples.

hidden.name: estimation noise per condition
paras: The paper introduces a named quantity that no one had formalized before: the coverage-density trade-off. Here is what it means. When you train a robot on demonstrated actions at a condition (a starting position), two sources of error hurt you. First, estimation error (also called density): if you have only one demo at that condition, random sensor noise means you did not learn the true action, only a noisy version. Repeating the demo at the same condition shrinks this error by averaging out the noise. Second, extrapolation error (also called coverage): if you have never shown the robot a condition, it must guess, and guessing from far away is risky. Adding more unique conditions shrinks this error.

The paper proves mathematically that there is an optimal balance. With budget N total demonstrations and d output dimensions, you should allocate roughly N^(1/(d+1)) unique conditions and repeat each one about d times. If you deviate from this balance either way (too few conditions, each repeated many times, or too many conditions, each repeated once), total error grows. The paper estimates this hidden noise level by running the base policy on probe trajectories and measuring how far its predicted action is from what a human would do.

heat.caption: Darker means more estimation noise. Anchors (repeated) are dark; boundaries (risk) are medium; unused regions are light.

reads.html: Estimation noise is the randomness left over when you train on just one noisy example. Repeating it at the same condition lets the robot average out the noise and see the true action.

The paper bounds the worst-case error over all conditions as a sum of bias and variance terms, showing that bias is proportional to 1/sqrt(K) where K is the repetition count at each condition, and variance grows with distance to the nearest anchor.

paras: The mechanism has two parts. First, repeated demonstrations at core anchors build a low-noise base policy. When the robot sees the same condition ten times with small random variations, it learns to ignore the noise and extract the reliable action pattern because the true action is the same every time (signal) while noise differs (random), so averaging across repetitions cancels noise and preserves signal.

Second, the base policy acts as a detector of risky regions. The paper uses teacher-forced deviation: give the base policy a human-demonstrated observation and see what action it outputs. If the output differs a lot from what the human actually did, that region is far from the anchors and the robot is uncertain. These high-deviation regions are the boundaries. By collecting new demonstrations specifically at those boundaries and training a small learnable residual (additional, lightweight adjustment layer) on top of the frozen base, the robot efficiently extends its competence without destabilizing what it already knows. The base policy stays fixed, so the core knowledge does not drift. The residual is trained with constraints (low-rank adapters), keeping it small so it can adapt to boundary quirks without overfitting to noise.

math.words: The total error (how far the learned action is from the true action, in the worst case) is bounded by a sum of two terms: a bias term that shrinks as you repeat demonstrations more at each condition, and a variance term that grows as conditions spread farther from covered anchors.
math.equation: E(K) <= C * sigma * sqrt(r*K/N) + L * h^(1/d) * K^(-1/d)
symbols: total error bound (how wrong the policy can be in the worst case)
a constant capturing the noise scale
output dimensionality (how many action numbers the robot outputs)
the worst-case distance from any condition to its nearest anchor
input dimensionality (how many numbers describe the robot state)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose you have N=100 total demos, d=5 state dimensions, and noise level sigma=1. The first term (bias) says error from noise is about 1 * sqrt(5 * K / 100) = sqrt(K/20). With K=100 unique conditions (spread wide), this is sqrt(5) ≈ 2.24. With K=10 unique conditions (anchors), this is sqrt(0.5) ≈ 0.71.

The second term (extrapolation) depends on how far the robot must extrapolate. Suppose L=1 and the worst boundary is distance h=0.2 from any anchor. Then error is about 0.2^(1/5) * K^(-1/5). With K=100, this is 0.2^0.2 * 100^(-0.2) ≈ 0.72 * 0.63 ≈ 0.45. With K=10, this is 0.2^0.2 * 10^(-0.2) ≈ 0.72 * 0.84 ≈ 0.60.

Total error with K=100 (spread wide) is 2.24 + 0.45 ≈ 2.69. Total error with K=10 (anchors) is 0.71 + 0.60 ≈ 1.31. The anchor strategy is 2x better, even though it covers fewer conditions. The balance comes from doing the remaining conditions via a boundary-mining residual, which only needs to learn small corrections.

math.note: The formula shows that error has two competing pieces: noise shrinks when you repeat (repeat more, sqrt term improves), but you cannot cover everything by repeating alone. The paper uses boundary mining to add coverage where it matters most, guided by extrapolation risk.

charts.title: Spread-wide strategy (100 unique positions, 1 demo each)
charts.note: Broad coverage looks good in theory. But noise from single examples destabilizes the learning, so success is unpredictable.

charts.title: Anchor-centric adaptation
charts.note: Fewer initially-covered regions, but repetition at anchors builds stable knowledge. Boundary mining adds coverage where the base policy is most uncertain.

items.html: If the anchor positions do not cover the range of tasks the robot will actually face, even repetition at anchors cannot build a good base. The paper assumes anchors are chosen to be representative core positions, but does not automate this choice.

items.b: Boundary mining fails if base policy is too bad.
items.html: Teacher-forced deviation relies on the base policy being informative: its mistakes should reveal where the robot is out of its depth. If the base is terrible, high-deviation regions are just noise, not true high-risk zones.

items.b: Residual adapters may overfit to small boundary sets.
items.html: If the boundary dataset is very small and the residual is too expressive, the constrained update can still memorize noise. The paper mitigates this with low-rank constraints, but the boundary set size still matters.

Anchors should be selected based on task structure (e.g., canonical grip positions, table corners) or by clustering real expert trajectories. This requires domain knowledge but ensures the base policy captures the core skill.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should show that anchor-centric allocation beats uniform spreading under a fixed budget. Set up a simulated or real robot reaching task with, say, a 5 by 5 grid of starting positions. Allocate 100 total demonstrations two ways: (1) spread-wide: 4 demos per position, one per position repeated twice, or one per position once with high noise; (2) anchor-centric: 2 anchors with 20 demos each, then boundary mining to add 10 more demos at the 2-3 highest-error grid cells. Train both policies and measure success rate across a test set of 25 random starting positions.
demo.metric_eq: robustness = mean success rate on test positions minus standard deviation of success; higher is better (both higher mean and lower variance matter)
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that the base policy (trained on anchors alone) is stable but limited, and the residual (trained on mined boundaries) extends it just enough, achieving higher success than spreading the same budget uniformly.
